polities.text: The Roman state after the expulsion of its kings, traditionally from 509 BC, governed by annually elected magistrates and the Senate. It grew from a city-state in Latium into the ruler of the whole Mediterranean, and ended in civil wars from which Augustus emerged as sole ruler.

The Roman state under emperors, from Augustus onward. At its height in the 2nd century it ruled from Britain to Egypt and Mesopotamia. It was divided for good into western and eastern halves in 395; the western half collapsed in the 5th century.
The western half of the Roman Empire after the division of 395, ruled from Milan and then Ravenna. It lost its provinces to Goths, Vandals, Franks and others, and its last emperor was deposed in 476.

The continuation of the Roman Empire in the east, with its capital at Constantinople, Greek in language and Orthodox Christian in religion. It recovered much of the west under Justinian, lost Syria and Egypt to the Arabs, and fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

A loose empire of hundreds of principalities, bishoprics and free cities in central Europe, centred on Germany, whose emperor was chosen by prince-electors. It is usually dated from the coronation of Otto I in 962 and was dissolved in 1806 under pressure from Napoleon.

The kingdom of the Franks, built by Clovis and his Merovingian successors in Gaul and expanded by the Carolingians. Under Charlemagne it covered most of western Europe; his grandsons divided it at Verdun in 843.
The Frankish realm at its greatest extent, after Charlemagne was crowned emperor in Rome in 800. It was partitioned among his grandsons and the parts became the cores of France and Germany.
The French monarchy, which grew from the lands of the Capetian kings around Paris into the most populous state in Europe. The monarchy was overthrown in 1792 during the French Revolution.
The kingdom created when the rulers of Wessex united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in the 10th century, conquered by the Normans in 1066. It united with Scotland in 1707 to form Great Britain.
The kingdom in the north of Britain, which kept its independence from England in the wars of the 13th and 14th centuries. It shared a monarch with England from 1603 and united with it in 1707.

The state formed by the union of England and Scotland in 1707. In this period it became the leading naval and colonial power and the first industrial country, and lost thirteen of its American colonies.

names: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
polities.text: Great Britain and Ireland under one parliament from 1801. It was the centre of the largest empire in history and the leading industrial and financial power of the 19th century.
polities.w: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

polities.text: The colonies, dominions, protectorates and other territories ruled from Britain. At its greatest extent, after the First World War, it covered about a quarter of the world's land and people; most of it became independent in the two decades after the Second World War.

The overseas possessions of the Spanish crown, begun with Columbus's voyages. In the 16th and 17th centuries it covered most of the Americas, the Philippines and parts of Europe; most of its American territories became independent in the 1810s and 1820s.

The first and longest-lived of the European overseas empires, built on forts and trading posts along the coasts of Africa, India and East Asia, and on Brazil. It began with the capture of Ceuta in 1415 and ended with the handover of Macau in 1999.
The Portuguese monarchy, independent of León from the 12th century. It led the European voyages of exploration in the 15th century and was replaced by a republic in 1910.

A federal republic of seven provinces that broke away from Spanish rule. In the 17th century it was Europe's leading trading and shipping nation, with a commercial empire in Asia and the Atlantic; it fell to French revolutionary armies in 1795.

A chartered trading company, founded in 1602, with the right to wage war, make treaties and govern territory in Asia. It ruled parts of Java, Ceylon, the Spice Islands and the Cape, and was dissolved in 1799.
An English trading company chartered in 1600 that came to rule most of India after its victory at Plassey. The British crown took over its territories after the rebellion of 1857.

The lands ruled by the Austrian branch of the House of Habsburg: Austria, Bohemia, Hungary and, at times, the southern Netherlands and parts of Italy. It was reorganised as the Austrian Empire in 1804.
The empire proclaimed by the Habsburg ruler Francis in 1804, a multinational state in central Europe. After defeat by Prussia it was reorganised as the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary in 1867.
The Dual Monarchy created in 1867, in which the Austrian and Hungarian halves shared a ruler, an army and a foreign policy. It broke up along national lines at the end of the First World War in 1918.
The kingdom of the Hohenzollern rulers of Brandenburg, crowned kings in 1701. It became a great power under Frederick the Great and united Germany under its leadership in 1871.

The German nation-state founded in 1871 under the Prussian king as emperor, with Bismarck as its first chancellor. It became the strongest industrial and military power on the continent and collapsed in defeat and revolution in 1918.
A league of German states set up by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 to replace the Holy Roman Empire, presided over by Austria. It ended with the Austro-Prussian War of 1866.

A union of the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania with an elected king and a powerful noble parliament, formed at Lublin in 1569. One of the largest states in Europe, it was partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria and disappeared in 1795.
A state that grew from the last pagan realm in Europe into a power ruling much of present-day Belarus and Ukraine. It was joined to Poland by a dynastic union and then by the Union of Lublin.

The Hungarian kingdom, founded with the coronation of Stephen I. Most of it was conquered by the Ottomans after 1526 and the rest passed to the Habsburgs, who ruled all of it from the end of the 17th century.

A federation of East Slavic principalities under the Rurikid dynasty, centred on Kiev, which adopted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium. It broke into rival principalities and was conquered by the Mongols, who sacked Kiev in 1240.
The principality around Moscow that grew under Mongol overlordship, threw it off under Ivan III and gathered the other Russian lands. Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547.
The Russian state from the coronation of Ivan IV as tsar in 1547. It expanded across Siberia to the Pacific and, under Peter the Great, to the Baltic; Peter proclaimed it an empire in 1721.
The empire proclaimed by Peter the Great in 1721, stretching from Poland to the Pacific and, for a time, Alaska. It was overthrown in the revolutions of 1917.

A federation of socialist republics under Communist Party rule, formed in 1922 from the former Russian Empire. It was one of the two superpowers of the Cold War and dissolved into fifteen states in 1991.
A merchant republic in northern Rus' governed by an assembly and elected officials, trading furs with the Hanseatic towns. Moscow annexed it in 1478.

The western part of the Mongol Empire, founded by Batu Khan, which ruled the steppe from the Danube to the Aral Sea and took tribute from the Russian principalities. It broke up into the khanates of Kazan, Astrakhan, Crimea and others.
A Tatar khanate on the Crimean peninsula and the steppe to its north, a successor of the Golden Horde and from the 1470s a vassal of the Ottoman Empire. Russia annexed it in 1783.

A state on the Baltic coast created by a German crusading order that conquered and converted the pagan Prussians. It was defeated by Poland and Lithuania at Grunwald and secularised as the Duchy of Prussia in 1525.

A maritime republic ruled by an elected doge and a closed merchant aristocracy. It dominated trade between Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, held Crete, Cyprus and the Dalmatian coast, and was ended by Napoleon in 1797.
A maritime republic and rival of Venice, with colonies and trading posts around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, later a banker to the Spanish crown.
The territories in central Italy ruled directly by the pope. They were annexed by the Kingdom of Italy, the last of them, Rome itself, in 1870.
A kingdom founded by the Norman Roger II in 1130, covering Sicily and southern Italy, where Latin, Greek and Arab cultures met. It was later ruled by German, French and Spanish dynasties.
The mainland half of the old Kingdom of Sicily, separate from the island after the Sicilian Vespers. It was ruled in turn by Angevin, Aragonese, Spanish and Bourbon kings.
The Bourbon kingdom formed by uniting Naples and Sicily after the Napoleonic Wars, the largest state in Italy before unification. Garibaldi conquered it and it joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.
The state of the House of Savoy, ruled from Turin, with Piedmont as its core. It led the unification of Italy, and its king became King of Italy in 1861.
The Italian state created by unification in 1861 under the House of Savoy. It was ruled by Mussolini's Fascists from 1922 and became a republic by referendum in 1946.

A union of Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands that built a Mediterranean empire including Sicily, Sardinia and Naples. The marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile joined it to Castile.
The largest of the Christian kingdoms of medieval Spain, which took most of the south from the Muslims and financed Columbus. With Aragon it formed the Spanish monarchy.
The Umayyad state in Muslim Spain after its ruler took the title of caliph in 929. Córdoba was then one of the largest cities in Europe; the caliphate broke into small taifa kingdoms in 1031.
The last Muslim state in Spain, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty from the Alhambra. Castile and Aragon conquered it in 1492.

A Berber religious movement from the Atlas mountains that overthrew the Almoravids and ruled the Maghreb and Muslim Spain. Its defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa opened southern Spain to the Christian kingdoms.
A Berber dynasty from the western Sahara that founded Marrakesh and ruled Morocco and Muslim Spain. It was overthrown by the Almohads.
A kingdom founded by the Visigoths in south-western Gaul and then Spain, with its capital at Toledo. It was destroyed by the Muslim conquest that began in 711.
The kingdom of Theodoric the Great and his successors in Italy, which kept much of Roman administration. It was destroyed by the armies of Justinian.
The kingdom set up by the Lombards who invaded Italy in 568, with its capital at Pavia. Charlemagne conquered it in 774.
A kingdom in Roman North Africa founded by the Vandals, who took Carthage and sacked Rome in 455. Justinian's general Belisarius destroyed it.
A union of the crowns of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch, formed in 1397. It ended when Sweden broke away under Gustav Vasa in 1523.
The union of the Danish and Norwegian crowns, with Iceland, Greenland and the Faroe Islands, ruled from Copenhagen. Denmark ceded Norway to Sweden in 1814.

Sweden in its age as a great power, when it ruled Finland, Estonia, Livonia and parts of northern Germany and intervened in the Thirty Years' War. It lost its Baltic provinces to Russia in the Great Northern War, which ended in 1721.
A league of Alpine valley communities and towns, traditionally dated from 1291, that won its independence from the Habsburgs. It was replaced by the French-backed Helvetic Republic in 1798.
The empire of Napoleon I, proclaimed in 1804. At its height it ruled or dominated most of continental Europe; it fell after the invasion of Russia and ended for good after Waterloo in 1815.

A Turkish dynasty's state that grew from a small principality in Anatolia into an empire over south-eastern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. It took Constantinople in 1453, reached its height in the 16th century, and was abolished in 1922.

The Seljuk Turkish state in Anatolia, founded after the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert, with its capital at Konya. It became a Mongol vassal and broke into small principalities, one of which was the Ottoman.
A Turkish dynasty that conquered Iran and Iraq, took Baghdad and ruled as sultans in the name of the Abbasid caliph. Its victory over Byzantium at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.
A state ruled from Cairo by sultans drawn from a caste of slave soldiers. It stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut, expelled the last crusaders, and was conquered by the Ottomans in 1517.
The dynasty of Saladin, who ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171, united Egypt and Syria and took Jerusalem from the crusaders. It was replaced in Egypt by its own Mamluk soldiers.
An Ismaili Shia caliphate that arose in North Africa in 909, conquered Egypt and founded Cairo as its capital. Saladin abolished it in 1171.

The dynasty that overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled the Islamic world from Baghdad, a centre of learning and trade. Its political power faded from the 9th century, and the Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258.
The first hereditary dynasty of caliphs, ruling from Damascus. Under it the Arab empire reached from Spain to the Indus; the Abbasids overthrew it in 750.
The caliphate of the first four successors of Muhammad. In three decades its armies conquered Arabia, Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Iran from the Byzantine and Sasanian empires.
The last Persian empire before Islam, founded by Ardashir I in 224, with Zoroastrianism as its state religion. It was the great rival of Rome and Byzantium and fell to the Arab conquest in 651.
An Iranian empire founded by the Arsacid dynasty, which took Iran and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids. It defeated Rome at Carrhae and was overthrown by the Sasanians in 224.
The first Persian empire, founded by Cyrus the Great, which ruled from the Aegean and Egypt to the Indus. Alexander the Great conquered it.
The largest of the kingdoms founded by Alexander's generals, stretching at first from Anatolia to Central Asia. It shrank under Parthian and Roman pressure to Syria, which Rome annexed.
The kingdom of Egypt under the Macedonian dynasty founded by Alexander's general Ptolemy, with its capital at Alexandria. It ended with the death of Cleopatra VII and Roman annexation.
A kingdom on the northern edge of the Greek world that Philip II made master of Greece. His son Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire; Rome ended the kingdom after the battle of Pydna.
A Phoenician colony in present-day Tunisia that became the leading trading and naval power of the western Mediterranean. It fought three wars with Rome, which destroyed the city in 146 BC.

The dynasty that reunited Iran in 1501 and made Twelver Shia Islam its state religion. Its capital Isfahan flourished under Abbas the Great; the state collapsed after an Afghan invasion and was replaced by Nader Shah in 1736.
The Turkic dynasty that ruled Iran from Tehran, losing the Caucasus to Russia and falling under British and Russian influence. Reza Shah replaced it in 1925.
The empire of Timur (Tamerlane), who from 1370 conquered Central Asia, Iran and Iraq and sacked Delhi. Under his successors Samarkand and Herat were centres of art and science.
The largest land empire in history, founded by Genghis Khan in 1206. His successors conquered China, Central Asia, Iran and Russia; by the late 13th century it had divided into four khanates.
The Mongol khanate in Iran and Iraq, founded by Hulagu, who destroyed Baghdad. Its rulers converted to Islam, and it broke up after 1335.
The Mongol khanate in Central Asia, named after Genghis Khan's second son. Timur rose to power in its western half.
The Mongol dynasty in China, proclaimed by Kublai Khan in 1271, which completed the conquest of the Song. It was driven back to the steppe by the Ming in 1368.

The dynasty that ruled China for four centuries after the short-lived Qin, with a break in the early 1st century. It extended Chinese rule into Central Asia, Korea and Vietnam, and gave its name to the Han Chinese; it ended in 220.

The first imperial dynasty of China, founded when the king of Qin conquered the other warring states and took the title of First Emperor. It standardised writing, weights and measures, and lasted only fifteen years.
A Chinese dynasty founded in 618, often seen as a high point of Chinese civilisation, with its capital at Chang'an. It was weakened by the An Lushan Rebellion and ended in 907.
A Chinese dynasty founded in 960, marked by commercial growth, printing, paper money and gunpowder weapons. It lost the north to the Jurchen Jin and was conquered by the Mongols in 1279.
The Chinese dynasty founded in 1368 after the expulsion of the Mongols. It rebuilt the Great Wall, sent Zheng He's fleets across the Indian Ocean, and fell to rebels and then the Manchus in 1644.

The last imperial dynasty of China, founded by the Manchus, who took Beijing in 1644. In the 18th century it ruled Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang as well as China; it was overthrown by the revolution that began in 1911 and ended in 1912.
An empire founded by the Khitan people of the steppe, ruling Mongolia, Manchuria and part of northern China. It was destroyed by the Jurchens.
A dynasty founded by the Jurchens of Manchuria in 1115, which destroyed the Liao and took northern China from the Song. The Mongols conquered it in 1234.
A state of the Tangut people in north-western China, founded in 1038. It was destroyed by the Mongols in 1227.
A confederation of nomadic peoples on the Mongolian steppe that raided and fought Han China for centuries. The Han broke its power in the 1st century.
The northernmost of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, which ruled northern Korea and much of Manchuria. It fell to an alliance of Silla and Tang China in 668.
One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, in the south-east, which with Tang help conquered Baekje and Goguryeo and unified most of the peninsula. It gave way to Goryeo in the 10th century.
One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, in the south-west, which passed Buddhism and continental culture on to Japan. Silla and Tang China conquered it in 660.
The dynasty that reunified Korea, founded in 918, from whose name the word Korea comes. It was a Mongol vassal for a century and was replaced by Joseon in 1392.
The Korean dynasty founded by Yi Seong-gye in 1392, with Confucianism as its state creed and Seoul as its capital. The Korean alphabet was created under King Sejong.
The military government of Japan under the Tokugawa family, based at Edo, founded in 1603. It kept the peace for two and a half centuries and closed the country to most foreign contact.

Japan from the Meiji Restoration of 1868, which industrialised rapidly and took Taiwan, Korea and Manchuria. Its war in China and the Pacific ended in defeat in 1945, and a new constitution took effect in 1947.
The second of Japan's three military governments, based in Kyoto. Its authority collapsed in the Ōnin War, which opened a century of fighting between regional lords.
Japan's first military government, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo at Kamakura. It beat off two Mongol invasions and fell in 1333.

A Hindu and Buddhist empire in mainland Southeast Asia, centred on Angkor, whose kings built Angkor Wat and a vast system of reservoirs. It is dated from 802 and declined after Thai attacks, the capital being abandoned in 1431.
A Malay maritime kingdom based at Palembang on Sumatra, which controlled trade through the Strait of Malacca and was a centre of Buddhist learning.
A Hindu-Buddhist empire based in eastern Java, founded in 1293, which claimed overlordship over much of the Indonesian archipelago in the 14th century.
A Thai kingdom founded in the mid-14th century, whose capital on the Chao Phraya river was one of the great trading cities of Asia. A Burmese army destroyed the capital in 1767.
The Thai kingdom ruled from Bangkok by the Chakri dynasty since 1782. It was the only state in Southeast Asia to escape colonial rule; absolute monarchy ended in 1932.
The Vietnamese kingdom in the Red River region, independent of China from the 10th century. It defeated Mongol and Ming invasions and expanded south at the expense of Champa.
A group of Hindu and later Muslim Cham kingdoms on the coast of central and southern Vietnam, gradually absorbed by Đại Việt.
The first kingdom to unite the Irrawaddy valley, the base of Burmese language and culture. Thousands of Buddhist temples were built at its capital before it broke up after Mongol invasions.
A Burmese dynasty that under Bayinnaung in the 16th century briefly ruled the largest empire in the history of Southeast Asia.
The last Burmese dynasty, founded in 1752, which destroyed Ayutthaya and fought off Qing invasions. Britain conquered it in three wars, the last in 1885.
A Malay sultanate that controlled the Strait of Malacca and became the main trading port of Southeast Asia and a centre for the spread of Islam. The Portuguese captured the city in 1511.
The first empire to rule most of the Indian subcontinent, founded by Chandragupta Maurya. Its third ruler Ashoka turned to Buddhism after the Kalinga war and had edicts carved on rocks and pillars.
An empire in northern India whose age is remembered as a classical period of Sanskrit literature, mathematics and art.
An empire founded by a Central Asian people in Bactria and northern India, which linked the Silk Road with the Indian Ocean and patronised Buddhism.
A Tamil dynasty of southern India which at its height in the 11th century ruled Sri Lanka and sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya. It ended in 1279.
A Hindu empire in southern India, founded in 1336, whose ruined capital is at Hampi. It was broken by the Deccan sultanates at Talikota.
A series of five Muslim dynasties ruling northern India from Delhi from 1206. Timur sacked Delhi at the end of the 14th century, and Babur ended the sultanate at Panipat in 1526.

A Muslim dynasty of Central Asian origin, founded by Babur in 1526, that ruled most of India under Akbar and his successors and built the Taj Mahal. It declined in the 18th century; the British deposed the last emperor in 1857.
A Hindu power from western India, founded by Shivaji in 1674, that took over much of the Mughal Empire in the 18th century. The British defeated it for the last time in 1818.
A state in the Punjab created by Ranjit Singh in 1799. The British annexed it in 1849 after two wars.
British crown rule in India, which replaced the East India Company in 1858. It ended in 1947 with independence and the partition into India and Pakistan.
An Afghan empire founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747, at first reaching from eastern Iran to northern India. It is regarded as the origin of the modern Afghan state.
A Turkic dynasty ruling from Ghazni in present-day Afghanistan. Mahmud of Ghazni raided deep into India in the early 11th century.
A Turkic dynasty that ruled Central Asia and Iran in the early 13th century. Genghis Khan destroyed it after its governor killed a Mongol caravan.
An Uzbek state in Transoxiana, a centre of Islamic learning, later ruled as an emirate. Russia made its successor a protectorate.
An Uzbek khanate in Khwarazm, south of the Aral Sea. It became a Russian protectorate in the 1870s and was abolished in 1920.
A khanate in the Fergana valley, founded in 1709. Russia annexed it in 1876.
A state of the Kazakh nomads of the steppe, founded in 1465 and divided into three hordes. Russia absorbed it in the 18th and 19th centuries.
The last great nomadic empire of the steppe, ruled by western Mongols. The Qing destroyed it in the 1750s.
The first steppe empire to use the name Turk, founded in the mid-6th century, which stretched from Manchuria to the Black Sea before dividing into eastern and western halves.
A Turkic people whose state controlled the steppe north of the Caucasus and the trade between the Baltic and the Islamic world. Part of its elite adopted Judaism.

The empire of the Assyrian kings in the early first millennium BC, which conquered the Near East from Egypt to Iran with a standing army and mass deportations. It fell to the Babylonians and Medes, who took Nineveh.
The last native Mesopotamian empire, founded in 626 BC. Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon and destroyed Jerusalem; Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BC.
An Anatolian people whose empire, ruled from Hattusa, fought Egypt at Kadesh and concluded with it one of the earliest surviving peace treaties. It collapsed around the end of the Bronze Age.
An ancient civilisation in south-western Iran with its capital at Susa, a neighbour and frequent enemy of the Mesopotamian states.
An Iron Age kingdom around Lake Van in the Armenian highlands, a rival of Assyria.
Egypt at the height of its power, under the 18th to 20th dynasties, when it ruled Nubia and much of the Levant. Its pharaohs included Hatshepsut, Akhenaten and Ramesses II.
A Nubian kingdom on the middle Nile, whose kings ruled Egypt as its 25th dynasty. From its later capital Meroë it traded with the Roman world.

The Christian empire of the Ethiopian highlands under the Solomonic dynasty, restored in 1270. It defeated Italy at Adwa, was occupied by Italy from 1936 to 1941, and ended after the overthrow of Haile Selassie in 1974.

The earliest known empire of the western Sahel, in present-day Mauritania and Mali, grown rich on the trade in gold and salt across the Sahara. It has no connection with the modern state that took its name.

A Mandinka empire founded by Sundiata Keita, which controlled the gold trade of West Africa. Its ruler Mansa Musa became famous for his pilgrimage to Mecca, and Timbuktu grew into a centre of learning.
The largest of the West African empires, centred on Gao on the Niger. A Moroccan army with firearms destroyed it at Tondibi in 1591.
A state around Lake Chad that lasted for about a thousand years, Muslim from the 11th century, and a terminus of trans-Saharan trade.
An Islamic state in northern Nigeria created by the jihad of Usman dan Fodio that began in 1804. Britain conquered it in 1903.
A kingdom of the Edo people in southern Nigeria, known for its bronze and ivory sculpture. A British expedition sacked Benin City in 1897. It is not the modern Republic of Benin.
A Yoruba empire in present-day south-western Nigeria, a major power of the 17th and 18th centuries with a strong cavalry.
An Akan empire in present-day Ghana, founded in 1701, rich in gold. It fought several wars with Britain and was annexed to the Gold Coast.
A kingdom in present-day Benin, a major supplier of captives to the Atlantic slave trade. France conquered it in the 1890s.
A kingdom south of the Congo river whose kings became Christian after contact with Portugal in the 1480s. It was weakened by civil war and the slave trade.
A Shona kingdom whose capital, Great Zimbabwe, has the largest ancient stone buildings in southern Africa. It traded gold to the Swahili coast.
A Shona kingdom between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers that succeeded Great Zimbabwe and traded gold with the Portuguese.
A kingdom in south-eastern Africa built by Shaka into the strongest military power of the region. It defeated a British army at Isandlwana in 1879 but lost the war.
The kingdom of the central highlands of Madagascar, which in the 19th century ruled most of the island. France annexed it in 1897.
An Omani Arab sultanate on the East African coast, separated from Oman in 1856, a centre of the clove and slave trades. It became a British protectorate and ended with the revolution of 1964.
A Muslim sultanate on the Blue Nile, founded in the early 16th century, with its capital at Sennar. Egypt conquered it in 1821.
An alliance of three city-states in the Valley of Mexico, led by Tenochtitlan, that took tribute from much of central Mexico. Cortés and his Indigenous allies destroyed it in 1521.

The largest state of the pre-Columbian Americas, expanding from Cusco after 1438 along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile, held together by roads and labour service. Pizarro captured its ruler in 1532 and took Cusco in 1533.

A civilisation of city-states in the Yucatán, Guatemala and Belize, with a writing system, a complex calendar and monumental temples. Its classic cities declined in the 9th century; the last independent Maya kingdom fell to Spain in 1697.
Spain's viceroyalty in North and Central America, ruled from Mexico City after the conquest of 1521, which also governed the Philippines. It ended with Mexican independence in 1821.
Spain's viceroyalty in South America, created in 1542 and ruled from Lima; the silver of Potosí made it the richest part of the empire. Spanish rule ended after the battle of Ayacucho in 1824.

names: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata
polities.text: The last Spanish viceroyalty, created in 1776 with its capital at Buenos Aires. Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Uruguay grew out of it.
polities.w: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

polities.text: A Spanish viceroyalty in northern South America, ruled from Bogotá. Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama grew out of it.
The republic created by Bolívar in 1819, uniting present-day Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. It broke into three states in 1831.
Independent Brazil under the emperors Pedro I and Pedro II, from 1822. Slavery was abolished in 1888 and a military coup made the country a republic in 1889.
The government formed in 1861 by eleven southern slave states that seceded from the United States. It was defeated in the Civil War and ceased to exist in 1865.
The kingdom founded by Kamehameha I, who began uniting the islands in 1795. Its last monarch, Queen Liliʻuokalani, was overthrown in 1893, and the United States annexed the islands five years later.
A maritime chiefdom centred on Tonga whose influence reached across much of western Polynesia at its height around the 13th century.
A confederacy of five, later six, nations in what is now New York State, bound by the Great Law of Peace. It was a major power in the wars between the French and British in North America.
The state of the South Slavs, created in 1918. It was a kingdom until the Second World War and a socialist federation under Tito afterwards; it broke up in war in 1991 and 1992.

A state created in 1918 from the Czech lands and Slovakia, formerly in Austria-Hungary. It was dismembered by Germany after the Munich Agreement of 1938, restored after the war, ruled by Communists from 1948, and divided peacefully at the end of 1992.
Germany's first democracy, founded after the revolution of 1918. It survived hyperinflation but not the Great Depression, and ended when Hitler took power in 1933.

Germany under the dictatorship of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party, from 1933. It started the Second World War in Europe, murdered six million Jews and millions of others, and was defeated and occupied in 1945.
The Communist state set up in the Soviet occupation zone of Germany in 1949. It built the Berlin Wall to stop emigration and joined the Federal Republic in 1990.

The republic that replaced the Qing dynasty in 1912. It was divided among warlords, partly reunited by the Nationalists, invaded by Japan, and defeated on the mainland by the Communists in 1949, after which its government moved to Taiwan.
Egypt under Ottoman sovereignty, from the conquest of 1517. In the 19th century Muhammad Ali and his heirs ruled it as a nearly independent state, and Britain occupied it from 1882.
The crusader state set up at Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade sacked the city in 1204. The Byzantines of Nicaea retook the city in 1261.
A Greek state on the south-eastern coast of the Black Sea, founded in 1204 and ruled by the Komnenos family. The Ottomans took it in 1461.
The largest of the crusader states, founded after the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099. Saladin captured the city in 1187; the kingdom's last stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291.
A state founded by Bulgars and Slavs south of the Danube, recognised by Byzantium in 681. It adopted Christianity and the Cyrillic script, and was conquered by Basil II in 1018.
The Bulgarian state restored by the revolt of the brothers Asen and Peter in 1185. The Ottomans conquered it at the end of the 14th century.
The empire proclaimed by Stefan Dušan in 1346, which for a time ruled much of the Balkans. It broke up after 1371.
The kingdom of the Czech lands within the Holy Roman Empire, hereditary from 1198. The Habsburgs ruled it from 1526 until 1918.
A Romanian principality north of the lower Danube, tributary to the Ottomans from the 15th century. It united with Moldavia in 1859 to form Romania.
A Romanian principality east of the Carpathians, at its height under Stephen the Great. It united with Wallachia in 1859.
A largely self-governing principality under Ottoman overlordship, formed from the eastern part of the old Kingdom of Hungary. It passed to the Habsburgs.
The united Georgian monarchy, formed in 1008, which reached its height under David the Builder and Queen Tamar. Mongol and Timurid invasions broke it, and it split into three kingdoms.
An Armenian state on the Mediterranean coast of Anatolia, allied with the crusaders, a kingdom from the end of the 12th century. The Mamluks conquered it in 1375.
A Tatar state on the middle Volga, a successor of the Golden Horde, founded in 1438. Ivan the Terrible conquered it in 1552.
A Tatar khanate at the mouth of the Volga. Russia conquered it in the 1550s, gaining the whole course of the river.
A Tatar khanate in western Siberia. Its conquest by Cossacks under Yermak opened Siberia to Russia.
A state of the Bulgars at the meeting of the Volga and Kama rivers, Muslim from the 10th century, living by the fur trade. The Mongols destroyed it.
The Christian kingdom formed in the mountains of northern Spain after the Muslim conquest, the starting point of the Reconquista. It became the Kingdom of León.
The successor of Asturias in north-western Spain. It was united for good with Castile in the 13th century.
A Basque kingdom on both sides of the western Pyrenees. Its southern part was conquered by Castile and Aragon in the early 16th century; the northern part passed to France.
A city-republic in Tuscany, a centre of banking and of the Renaissance, dominated from the 15th century by the Medici family. It became a duchy in 1532.
A state in northern Italy ruled by the Visconti and Sforza families, a duchy from 1395. It passed to Spain and then Austria.
A duchy of the French crown whose Valois dukes in the 14th and 15th centuries added Flanders and most of the Low Countries, making one of the richest states in Europe.
A league of German states under Napoleon's protection, formed in 1806 as the Holy Roman Empire ended. It collapsed after his defeat at Leipzig in 1813.
A Polish state created by Napoleon in 1807 from lands Prussia had taken in the partitions. The Congress of Vienna divided it in 1815.
The Kingdom of Poland created at the Congress of Vienna in 1815, with the Russian tsar as king. It lost its autonomy after the risings of the 19th century.
The largest of the south German states, a kingdom from 1806, ruled by the Wittelsbach family. It joined the German Empire in 1871 and its monarchy fell in 1918.
Romania as a monarchy, proclaimed in 1881. It gained Transylvania and Bessarabia after the First World War; the king was forced to abdicate in 1947.
Sicily under Muslim rule, with its capital at Palermo, from the 9th century. The Normans completed their conquest of the island in 1091.
The kingdom of the West Saxons in southern England. Under Alfred the Great it resisted the Vikings, and its kings went on to unite England.
The first Muslim dynasty of Morocco, founded in 788 by a descendant of the Prophet, which established the city of Fez.
A Berber dynasty that replaced the Almohads in Morocco and ruled from Fez.
A Moroccan dynasty that drove the Portuguese from most of the coast, defeated a Portuguese invasion at Alcácer Quibir and conquered Songhai.
The dynasty that ruled Tunisia and eastern Algeria from Tunis after breaking with the Almohads. The Ottomans ended it in 1574.
An Arab dynasty that ruled Tunisia for the Abbasids from 800 and conquered Sicily. The Fatimids overthrew it in 909.
An Ottoman province in North Africa that was in practice a self-governing state, known for its corsairs. France invaded it in 1830.
A Christian Nubian kingdom on the middle Nile, with its capital at Old Dongola, which held off the Arab conquest and lasted for many centuries.
The southernmost of the Christian kingdoms of medieval Nubia, around the meeting of the Blue and White Niles.
A Muslim sultanate in the west of present-day Sudan. Britain annexed it to Sudan in 1916.
A Muslim sultanate in the Horn of Africa whose leader Ahmad Gragn overran most of Christian Ethiopia in the 16th century.
A kingdom on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, the most powerful state of the region in the 19th century, which gave its name to Uganda.
A state in the savanna of the south-eastern Congo basin, known for its system of sacred kingship.
A confederation of states in the southern Congo basin and neighbouring Angola and Zambia, trading in ivory, copper and slaves.
A Shona state on the Zimbabwean plateau that drove the Portuguese from the interior.
A Boer republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers, independent from 1854. Britain annexed it in the Second Boer War, which ended in 1902.
The Boer republic north of the Vaal river, recognised by Britain in 1852, where gold was found on the Witwatersrand. Britain annexed it in the Second Boer War.
The colony founded by the Dutch East India Company at the Cape of Good Hope in 1652 and taken by Britain during the Napoleonic Wars. It joined the Union of South Africa in 1910.
The state built by Samori Ture in the highlands of Guinea, which resisted the French for many years until his capture at the end of the century.
A Buddhist dynasty ruling Bengal and Bihar, patrons of the great monastic universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila.
A dynasty of the Deccan that was one of the great powers of India in the 9th century and had the Kailasa temple at Ellora cut from the rock.
The first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan, founded in 1347. It broke up into five sultanates.
An independent Muslim kingdom in Bengal, wealthy from textiles and trade. The Mughals conquered it in 1576.
A kingdom in the Brahmaputra valley founded by a Tai prince in 1228, which beat off Mughal invasions. It passed to the British in 1826.
A south Indian kingdom that under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan fought four wars against the British East India Company.
The state of the Nizams in the Deccan, founded in 1724, the largest princely state of British India. India annexed it in 1948.
The last independent kingdom of Sri Lanka, in the central highlands, which outlasted Portuguese and Dutch rule on the coast. Britain took it in 1815.
The kingdom created when the Gorkha ruler Prithvi Narayan Shah conquered the Kathmandu valley in 1768. The monarchy was abolished in 2008.
The empire of the Yarlung kings, which at its height rivalled Tang China, held the oasis towns of the Silk Road and adopted Buddhism. It broke up in the 9th century.
A kingdom in present-day Yunnan that fought both Tang China and Tibet. It fell in 902.
A Buddhist kingdom in Yunnan, founded in 937. The Mongols conquered it in 1253.
A kingdom in Manchuria and northern Korea founded in 698 by former subjects of Goguryeo. The Khitans destroyed it in 926.
An island kingdom, united in 1429, that prospered as a go-between in the trade of China, Japan and Southeast Asia. Japan annexed it in 1879.
The "kingdom of a million elephants", the Lao state on the middle Mekong. It split into three kingdoms in 1707.
A northern Thai kingdom centred on Chiang Mai, later under Burmese rule.
An early Thai kingdom, founded in 1238 and remembered for King Ramkhamhaeng and the Thai script. Ayutthaya absorbed it in 1438.
The last Vietnamese dynasty, which united the country from Huế in 1802. France made it a protectorate in the 1880s, and its last emperor abdicated in 1945.
The last major independent Javanese kingdom, which under Sultan Agung ruled most of Java. The Dutch East India Company divided it in 1755.
A sultanate at the northern tip of Sumatra, a centre of Islamic learning and the pepper trade. It fought the Dutch for thirty years before its sultan surrendered in 1903.
The Dutch colony that took over the possessions of the Dutch East India Company in 1800 and grew to cover the Indonesian archipelago. The Netherlands recognised Indonesian independence in 1949.
The federation of French colonies and protectorates in Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, formed in 1887. French rule ended in 1954 after the defeat at Dien Bien Phu.
The French colonies in North America, from the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes down the Mississippi to Louisiana. France lost them to Britain and Spain in 1763.
The Dutch colony on the Hudson river, with New Amsterdam as its main town. The English took it in the 1660s and the Dutch gave it up by treaty in 1667.
Russia's colony in Alaska, run by the Russian-American Company from 1799 for the fur trade. Russia sold it to the United States in 1867.
The state formed when settlers in Texas broke away from Mexico in 1836. The United States annexed it in 1845, and the transfer was completed in 1846.
Independent Mexico under Agustín de Iturbide, who was crowned emperor. He abdicated in 1823 and a republic followed.
A federation of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica, formed in 1823 after independence. It broke up in civil wars.
A union of Peru and Bolivia created by Andrés de Santa Cruz in 1836. Chile and Argentina went to war against it, and it was dissolved in 1839.

names: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata
polities.text: The state that grew out of the May Revolution of 1810 in Buenos Aires, the forerunner of Argentina.

polities.text: A group of chiefdoms in the highlands of present-day Colombia, known for their goldwork, the source of the legend of El Dorado.
